newsitem.title: FRANCE: French ballot on Sunday holds bourse hostage.
newsitem.headline: French ballot on Sunday holds bourse hostage.

text.p: Share traders fearing a win by the Socialists in the second round of the French parliamentary election on Sunday savagely marked down prices on Friday and warned of further falls next week.

A resurgent Socialist party has caused alarm among international investors who are anxious over the left's hostility to privatisations, company restructurings and private pension funds, all of which are market idols.
"A left win would further weaken the market," said Elisabetta Castelli, head of international equity sales at CDC Bourse. "If it's a right win, there is substantial upside."

The blue-chip CAC 40 share index was down 0.68 percent at 2,561 at 1025 GMT, with traders citing private opinion polls as cause for concern. The index dropped over 1.5 percent within 10 minutes, bringing this week's loss to over 7.5 percent.
Brokerage Paribas Capital Markets said it saw the share index fall to 2,500 on Monday if the left comes to power but sees that as a level to start buying French shares.

But a Socialist administration, inclined to keep the generous social security system and cutting working hours, could mean a five percent discount to share prices compared to the level they could reach if a conservative government were re-elected, said Paribas.

The Socialists have said they want to create 700,000 jobs, half coming from the public sector, while former Socialist prime minister Laurent Fabius said on Friday a left government would not raise taxes or spending to pay for its policies.

One broker estimated a three percent drop on Monday if there were a left victory, but the fall could be smaller if it were a clear Socialist majority without requiring support from the Communist party.

Paribas sees a two thirds chance of the Socialists and Communists winning, whereas before the first round voting last Sunday, it reckoned there was a 60 percent probability the centre-right RPR-UDF coalition would be returned.
However, another broker thought the share index could rise to 2,850 by the end of September after an initial fall on Monday to 2,500 as the market reacts adversely to a Socialist win.
The 2,500 level was being increasingly eyed as an important support level, as the idea of a left triumph took increasing hold on the market, said a share trader.

If the bourse closes around 2,500 on Friday, that would help position it for any Socialist electoral gain and limit the upset on Monday. "A Monday fall wouldn't be so heavy if we settle around 2,500 today," he said.
Shares in defence electronics firm Thomson-CSF were down 2.26 percent at 164.2 francs as hopes dwindled for the sale of the state's 58 percent stake as planned by the conservative government.

Some market operators, however, are hoping that once in power any Socialist government would moderate its stance and face up to the needs of budgetary rigour in order to join the single European currency in 1999.
